claims.claim: Additional studies have supported Ctenophora as the sister group to remaining metazoans.
claims.source: and subsequently by additional studies (Hejnol et al., 2009; Moroz et al., 2014; NISC Comparative Sequencing Program et al., 2013; Whelan et al., 2015; Whelan et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Some researchers have suggested that the Ctenophora-sister result arises from artifacts such as inadequate taxon sampling, flawed matrix husbandry, and use of poorly fitting substitution models.
claims.source: Others have suggested that this result arises from artifacts with potentially additive effects, such as inadequate taxon sampling, flawed matrix husbandry (undetected paralogy or contamination), and use of poorly fitting substitution models (Philippe et al., 2009; Pick et al., 2010; Pisani et al., 2015; Simion et al., 2017; Feuda et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Philippe et al., 2009; Pick et al., 2010; Pisani et al., 2015; Simion et al., 2017; Feuda et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Using different sets of genes can lead to different phylogenetic conclusions, with only a small number sometimes sufficient to drive one result or another.
claims.source: A third view has emphasized that using different sets of genes can lead to different conclusions, with only a small number sometimes sufficient to drive one result or another (Nosenko et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nosenko et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The phylogenetic controversy has spurred contemplation of possibly independent origins of several hallmark traits such as striated muscles, digestive systems, and nervous systems.
claims.source: This controversy, regardless of its eventual resolution, has spurred serious contemplation of possibly independent origins of several hallmark traits such as striated muscles, digestive systems, and nervous systems (Moroz et al., 2014; Dayraud et al., 2012; Hejnol and Martín-Durán, 2015; Liebeskind et al., 2017; Moroz and Kohn, 2016; Presnell et al., 2016; Steinmetz et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: New sequences and analyses focusing on the position of Placozoa have been slow to emerge.
claims.source: Driven by this controversy, new genomic and transcriptomic data from sponges, ctenophores, and metazoan outgroups have accrued, while new sequences and analyses focusing on the position of Placozoa have been slow to emerge.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' assessment.

claims.claim: The study provides draft genomes from three putative placozoan species that span the root of this clade's known diversity.
claims.source: Here, we provide a novel test of the phylogenetic position of placozoans, adding draft genomes from three putative species that span the root of this clade's known diversity (Eitel et al., 2013) (Table 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 and a citation to Eitel et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Orthology assignment yielded 4294 gene trees with at least 20 sequences each, sampling all five major metazoan clades and outgroups.
claims.source: Orthology assignment on sets of predicted proteomes derived from 59 genome and transcriptome assemblies yielded 4294 gene trees with at least 20 sequences each, sampling all five major metazoan clades and outgroups
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the orthology assignment procedure.

claims.claim: From the 4294 gene trees, 1388 well-aligned orthologues were obtained.
claims.source: from which we obtained 1388 well-aligned orthologues
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the alignment procedure.

claims.claim: A set of 430 most-informative orthologues were selected on the basis of tree-likeness scores.
claims.source: Within this set, individual maximum-likelihood (ML) gene trees were constructed, and a set of 430 most-informative orthologues were selected on the basis of tree-likeness scores (Misof et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the selection procedure with a citation to Misof et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The 430-gene matrix yielded an amino-acid matrix of 73,547 residues with 37.55% gaps or missing data.
claims.source: This yielded an amino-acid matrix of 73,547 residues with 37.55% gaps or missing data
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the matrix characteristics.

claims.claim: Bayesian analyses of the 430-gene matrix place Cnidaria and Placozoa as sister groups with full posterior probability under the CAT + GTR + Г4 model.
claims.source: Our Bayesian analyses of this matrix place Cnidaria and Placozoa as sister groups with full posterior probability under the general site-heterogeneous CAT + GTR + Г4 model (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and describes the results of Bayesian analysis.

claims.claim: Under ML inference with the C60 +LG + FO + R4 profile mixture model, Cnidaria + Placozoa is recovered, albeit with more marginal resampling support.
claims.source: Under ML inference with the C60 +LG + FO + R4 profile mixture model (Wang et al., 2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we again recover Cnidaria + Placozoa, albeit with more marginal resampling support.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Both Bayesian and ML analyses show little internal branch diversity within Placozoa.
claims.source: Both Bayesian and ML analyses show little internal branch diversity within Placozoa.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from both types of analyses.

claims.claim: Deleting all newly-added placozoan genomes from the analysis has no effect on topology and only a marginal effect on support in ML analysis.
claims.source: Accordingly, deleting all newly-added placozoan genomes from our analysis has no effect on topology and only a marginal effect on support in ML analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and describes the results of a sensitivity analysis.

claims.claim: Quartet-based concordance analyses show no evidence of strong phylogenetic conflicts among ML gene trees in the 430-gene set.
claims.source: Quartet-based concordance analyses (Zhou, 2017) show no evidence of strong phylogenetic conflicts among ML gene trees in this 430-gene set (Figure 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and a citation to Zhou, 2017.

claims.claim: Internode certainty metrics are close to 0 for many key clades including Cnidaria + Placozoa, indicating that support for some ancient relationships may be masked by gene-tree estimation errors.
claims.source: although internode certainty metrics are close to 0 for many key clades including Cnidaria + Placozoa, indicating that support for some ancient relationships may be masked by gene-tree estimation errors, emerging only in combined analysis (Gatesy and Baker, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gatesy and Baker, 2005 and describes the interpretation of internode certainty metrics.

claims.claim: Compositional heterogeneity of amino-acid frequencies along the tree is a source of phylogenetic error not modelled by even complex site-heterogeneous substitution models such as CAT+GTR.
claims.source: Compositional heterogeneity of amino-acid frequencies along the tree is a source of phylogenetic error not modelled by even complex site-heterogeneous substitution models such as CAT+GTR (Blanquart and Lartillot, 2008; Foster, 2004; Lartillot and Philippe, 2004; Lartillot et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Previous analyses have shown that placozoans and choanoflagellates deviate strongly from the mean amino-acid composition of Metazoa.
claims.source: Furthermore, previous analyses (Nosenko et al., 2013) have shown that placozoans and choanoflagellates in particular, both of which taxa our matrix samples intensively, deviate strongly from the mean amino-acid composition of Metazoa
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nosenko et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Deviation from mean amino-acid composition may be a result of genomic GC content discrepancies.
claims.source: perhaps as a result of genomic GC content discrepancies
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the cause of compositional deviation.

claims.claim: Analysis of the Dayhoff-6 recoded matrix under the CAT + GTR model recovered full support for Cnidaria + Placozoa.
claims.source: Analysis of this recoded matrix under the CAT + GTR model again recovered full support (pp = 1) for Cnidaria + Placozoa (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 and describes the results of analysis on the recoded matrix.

claims.claim: Under Dayhoff-6 recoding, the only major change is in the relative positions of Ctenophora and Porifera, with Porifera constituting the sister group to all other animals with full support.
claims.source: Indeed, under Dayhoff-6 recoding, the only major change is in the relative positions of Ctenophora and Porifera, with the latter here constituting the sister group to all other animals with full support.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the Dayhoff-6 recoded analysis.

claims.claim: Similar recoding-driven effects on relative positions of Porifera and Ctenophora have been seen in other recent work.
claims.source: Similar recoding-driven effects on relative positions of Porifera and Ctenophora have also been seen in other recent work (Feuda et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Feuda et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Recoding-driven effects have been interpreted to indicate a role for compositional bias in misplacing Ctenophora as sister group to all other animals.
claims.source: and have been interpreted to indicate a role for compositional bias in misplacing Ctenophora as sister group to all other animals
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of recoding effects in the literature.

claims.claim: Many research groups have consistently reported strong support for Planulozoa under the CAT + GTR model using good taxon sampling and genome-scale datasets.
claims.source: Many research groups, using good taxon sampling and genome-scale datasets, and even recently including data from a new divergent placozoan species (Whelan et al., 2017; Feuda et al., 2017; Eitel, 2017), have consistently reported strong support for Planulozoa under the CAT + GTR model.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Whelan et al., 2017; Feuda et al., 2017; Eitel, 2017.

claims.claim: A supermatrix constructed using complete sequences of 303 pan-eukaryote BUSCOs shows full support for Planulozoa in both amino-acid and Dayhoff-6 recoded alphabets.
claims.source: Indeed, when we construct a supermatrix from our predicted peptide catalogues using a different strategy, relying on complete sequences of 303 pan-eukaryote 'Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs' (BUSCOs) (Simão et al., 2015), we also see full support in a CAT + GTR + Г analysis for Planulozoa, in both amino-acid (Figure 3a) and Dayhoff-6 recoded alphabets (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by references to Figure 3a and 3b and a citation to Simão et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Both the initial 430-gene matrix and the 303-gene BUSCO matrix fail posterior predictive tests.
claims.source: Both the initial 430-gene matrix and the 303-gene BUSCO matrix fail these tests
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from posterior predictive tests.

claims.claim: The BUSCO matrix fails posterior predictive tests more profoundly than the 430-gene matrix, with z-scores in the range of 330–340 versus 176–187.
claims.source: but the BUSCO matrix fails it more profoundly, with z-scores (measuring mean-squared across-taxon heterogeneity) scoring in the range of 330–340, in contrast to the range of 176–187 seen in the 430-gene matrix (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 2 and describes the results of posterior predictive tests.

claims.claim: A large amount of the global difference in z-scores between matrices can be attributed to placozoans, with additional contributions from choanoflagellates and select isolated representatives of other clades.
claims.source: Furthermore, inspecting z-scores for individual taxa in representative chains from both matrices shows that a large amount of this global difference in z-scores can be attributed to placozoans, with additional contributions from choanoflagellates and select isolated representatives of other clades (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3C and describes the results of inspecting individual taxon z-scores.

claims.claim: At a conservative significance threshold of α = 0.10, the majority (764 genes or ~55%) of the 1388 gene set is identified as compositionally biased by a null-simulation test.
claims.source: Remarkably, at a conservative significance threshold of α = 0.10, the majority (764 genes or ~55%) of this gene set is identified as compositionally biased by this test
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the null-simulation test for compositional bias.

claims.claim: The null-simulation test for compositional bias is less prone to Type II errors than the more conventional X test.
claims.source: This test, which compares the real data to a null distribution of amino-acid frequencies simulated along assumed gene trees with a substitution model using a single composition vector, is less prone to Type II errors than the more conventional X (Grell and Benwitz, 1971) test (Foster, 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foster, 2004.

claims.claim: Analysis of the test-passing supermatrix shows strong support for Cnidaria + Placozoa.
claims.source: Building informative matrices from gene sets on either side of this significance threshold, and again applying both CAT + GTR mixture models and ML profile mixtures, we see strong support for Cnidaria + Placozoa in the test-passing supermatrix
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from analysis of the test-passing supermatrix.

claims.claim: Analysis of the test-failing supermatrix shows strong support for Cnidaria + Bilateria.
claims.source: and conversely, strong support for Cnidaria + Bilateria in the test-failing supermatrix (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by references to Figure 4 and its supplements and describes the results from analysis of the test-failing supermatrix.

claims.claim: In trees built through CAT + GTR + Г4 analysis of the test-failing supermatrix, full support is observed for Porifera as sister to all other animals in both amino-acid and Dayhoff-6 alphabets.
claims.source: Interestingly, in trees built through CAT + GTR + Г4 analysis of the test-failing supermatrix (Figure 4A,C), in both amino-acid and Dayhoff-6 alphabets, we also observe full support for Porifera as sister to all other animals.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by references to Figure 4A and 4C and describes the results from CAT + GTR + Г4 analysis.

claims.claim: Analysis of the test-failing amino acid matrix under a profile mixture model recovers support for Ctenophora as sister to all other animals.
claims.source: In contrast, analysis of this amino acid matrix under a profile mixture model recovers support for Ctenophora in this position (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and describes the results from profile mixture model analysis.

claims.claim: For the test-failing alignment, compositional heterogeneity need not be invoked to explain why outcomes differ among analyses, as both CAT + GTR and the C60 +LG + FO + R4 profile mixture model assume a single composition vector over time.
claims.source: indicating that, at least for this alignment, compositional heterogeneity need not be invoked to explain why outcomes differ among analyses, as some have argued (Feuda et al., 2017): both CAT + GTR and the C60 +LG + FO + R4 profile mixture model assume a single composition vector over time, but the CAT + GTR model is better able to accommodate site-heterogeneous substitution patterns (Lartillot et al., 2013; Quang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feuda et al., 2017; Lartillot et al., 2013; Quang et al., 2008 and involves inference about model assumptions.

claims.claim: Dayhoff-6 recoding appears impactful only for the test-passing supermatrix, where it obviates support for Ctenophora-sister in favour of Porifera-sister.
claims.source: In the context of this experiment, Dayhoff-6 recoding appears impactful only for the test-passing supermatrix (Figure 4B,D), where it obviates support for Ctenophora-sister (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) in favour of (albeit, with marginal support) Porifera-sister (Figure 4D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by references to Figure 4B, 4D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and describes the results from Dayhoff-6 recoding.

claims.claim: Dayhoff-6 recoding diminishes support for Placozoa + Cnidaria in the test-passing supermatrix, perhaps reflecting the inherent information loss of using a reduced amino-acid alphabet.
claims.source: and also diminishes support for Placozoa + Cnidaria (in contrast to the 430-gene matrix; Figure 2), perhaps reflecting the inherent information loss of using a reduced amino-acid alphabet for this relatively shorter matrix.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 and involves speculation about the cause of diminished support.

claims.claim: A possible hidden variable related to phylogenetic discordance is mean trimmed alignment length, with both the test-passing and the original 430-gene matrix composed of considerably shorter alignments than the test-failing and the 303-gene BUSCO matrix.
claims.source: A possible hidden variable related to the phylogenetic discordance we describe, the precise significance of which remains unclear, is mean trimmed alignment length: both the test-passing and the original 430-gene matrix are composed of considerably shorter alignments than the test-failing and the 303-gene BUSCO matrix (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a potential confounding variable based on the authors' observations.

claims.claim: Alignment length has been previously shown to be predictive of a number of other metrics of phylogenetic relevance.
claims.source: Indeed, alignment length has been previously shown to be predictive of a number of other metrics of phylogenetic relevance (Shen et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shen et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The phylogenetic link between cnidarians and placozoans seen in gene sets less influenced by compositional bias will require further testing with other analyses and data modalities.
claims.source: The previously cryptic phylogenetic link between cnidarians and placozoans seen in gene sets less influenced by compositional bias will require further testing with other analyses and data modalities, such as rare genomic changes
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the need for further validation of the findings.

claims.claim: Many workers presume that placozoans must have a still-unobserved, more typical development and life cycle, or else are merely oddities that have experienced wholesale secondary simplification.
claims.source: Many workers, citing the incompletely known development (Eitel et al., 2011; Pearse and Voigt, 2007) and relatively bilaterian-like gene content of placozoans (Srivastava et al., 2008; Eitel, 2017), presume that these organisms must have a still-unobserved, more typical development and life cycle (DuBuc et al., 2018), or else are merely oddities that have experienced wholesale secondary simplification, having scant significance to any evolutionary path outside their own.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and describes a common view in the field.

claims.claim: Much work on cnidarian models in the evo-devo paradigm is predicated on the notion that cnidarians and bilaterians share many homologous morphological features.
claims.source: Indeed, it is tempting to interpret this new phylogenetic position as further bolstering such hypotheses, as much work on cnidarian models in the evo-devo paradigm is predicated on the notion that cnidarians and bilaterians share, more or less, many homologous morphological features, viz. axial organization (Genikhovich and Technau, 2017; DuBuc et al., 2018), nervous systems (Liebeskind et al., 2017; Moroz and Kohn, 2016; Kelava et al., 2015; Kristan, 2016; Arendt et al., 2016), basement-membrane lined epithelia (Fidler et al., 2017; Leys and Riesgo, 2012), musculature (Steinmetz et al., 2012), embryonic germ-layer organisation (Steinmetz et al., 2017), and internal digestion (Presnell et al., 2016; Putnam et al., 2007; Hejnol and Martindale, 2008; Martindale and Hejnol, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: The authors hesitate to dismiss placozoans a priori as irrelevant to understanding early bilaterian evolution, as they have equal status to cnidarians as an immediate extant outgroup.
claims.source: While we do not argue, as some have done (Schierwater, 2005; Syed and Schierwater, 2002), that placozoans resemble hypothetical metazoan ancestors, we hesitate to dismiss them a priori as irrelevant to understanding early bilaterian evolution in particular: although apparently simpler and less diverse, placozoans nonetheless have equal status to cnidarians as an immediate extant outgroup.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of the authors' perspective on the significance of placozoans, with citations to Schierwater, 2005; Syed and Schierwater, 2002.

claims.claim: The authors see value in testing assumed hypotheses of homology by extending pairwise comparisons between bilaterians and cnidarians to include placozoans.
claims.source: Rather, we see value in testing assumed hypotheses of homology, character by character, by extending pairwise comparisons between bilaterians and cnidarians to include placozoans
claims.evidence: This is a statement of the authors' perspective on future research directions.

claims.claim: Recent progress has been made in reducing the disparity in knowledge between placozoans and other taxa using methods such as in situ hybridization, image analysis, and single-cell RNA-seq.
claims.source: an agenda which demands reducing the large disparity in embryological, physiological, and molecular genetic knowledge between these taxa, towards which recent progress has been made using both established methods such as in situ hybridization (DuBuc et al., 2018) and image analysis (Varoqueaux, 2018), as well as new technologies such as single-cell RNA-seq (Sebé-Pedrós, 2018a; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2018b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to DuBuc et al., 2018; Varoqueaux, 2018; Sebé-Pedrós, 2018a; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2018b.

claims.claim: Characters that can be validated as homologous between Bilateria and Cnidaria must have originated earlier in animal evolution than previously appreciated.
claims.source: Conversely, we emphasize another implication of this phylogeny: characters that can be validated as homologous at any level between Bilateria and Cnidaria must have originated earlier in animal evolution than previously appreciated
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic position of placozoans.

claims.claim: Homologous characters between Bilateria and Cnidaria should either cryptically occur in modern placozoans or else have been lost at some point in their ancestry.
claims.source: and should either cryptically occur in modern placozoans or else have been lost at some point in their ancestry.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic position of placozoans.

claims.claim: Paleobiological scenarios of early animal evolution founded on phylogenetically-informed interpretations of Ediacaran fossil forms and molecular clock estimates may require re-examination.
claims.source: In this light, paleobiological scenarios of early animal evolution founded on inherently phylogenetically-informed interpretations of Ediacaran fossil forms (Cavalier-Smith, 2018; Cavalier-Smith, 2017; Dufour and McIlroy, 2018; Sperling and Vinther, 2010; Evans et al., 2017) and molecular clock estimates (Cunningham et al., 2017; dos Reis et al., 2015; Dohrmann and Wörheide, 2017; Erwin et al., 2011) may require re-examination.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and involves inference about the implications of the phylogenetic findings.

claims.claim: Haplotype H4 and H6 placozoans were collected from water tables at the Kewalo Marine Laboratory, University of Hawaii-Manoa, Honolulu, Hawaii in October 2016.
claims.source: Haplotype H4 and H6 placozoans were collected from water tables at the Kewalo Marine Laboratory, University of Hawaii-Manoa, Honolulu, Hawaii in October 2016.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the sampling location and date.

claims.claim: Haplotype H11 placozoans were collected from the Mediterranean 'Anthias' show tank in the Palma de Mallorca Aquarium, Mallorca, Spain in June 2016.
claims.source: Haplotype H11 placozoans were collected from the Mediterranean 'Anthias' show tank in the Palma de Mallorca Aquarium, Mallorca, Spain in June 2016.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the sampling location and date.

claims.claim: The stringent metagenomics binning procedure and the very low proportion of multiple orthologue hits in the BUSCO2 assessment attest to the lack of evidence for residual non-placozoan contamination within the scaffolds used for gene prediction.
claims.source: Both the stringent metagenomics binning procedure (a procedure also expedient in other holobiont organisms (Celis et al., 2018)) and the very low proportion of multiple orthologue hits in the BUSCO2 assessment (Table 1) attest to the lack of evidence for residual non-placozoan contamination within the scaffolds used for gene prediction.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 and a citation to Celis et al., 2018, and describes quality control measures.

claims.claim: Support for the Cnidaria + Bilateria clade can be assigned to compositional heterogeneity as a source of systematic error.
claims.source: We demonstrate that a majority of genes show evidence of compositional heterogeneity, and that support for the Cnidaria + Bilateria clade can be assigned to this source of systematic error.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings regarding systematic error.

claims.claim: It is possible to obtain strong support for either a sister-group relationship between Cnidaria and Placozoa, or for Cnidaria and Bilateria, depending on the orthologues selected to construct the matrix.
claims.source: Using site-heterogeneous substitution models, we show that it is possible to obtain strong support, in both amino acid and reduced-alphabet matrices, for either a sister-group relationship between Cnidaria and Placozoa, or for Cnidaria and Bilateria as seen in most published work to date, depending on the orthologues selected to construct the matrix.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's main finding.

results.result: The study generated draft genomes from three placozoan haplotypes (H4, H6, H11) collected from Hawaii and Spain. Quality control measures including metagenomics binning and BUSCO assessment indicate minimal contamination in the assembled scaffolds used for gene prediction.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C63-C65 describe the sampling, assembly, and quality control of new placozoan genomes. The methods are clearly documented with specific locations and dates (C63-C64), and quality metrics in Table 1 support the lack of contamination (C65). These are standard genomic methods appropriately applied.

results.result: Orthology assignment from 59 proteomes yielded 4294 gene trees, from which 1388 well-aligned orthologues were obtained. A subset of 430 most-informative orthologues was selected based on tree-likeness scores, yielding a 73,547 amino acid matrix with 37.55% gaps.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C24 describe the computational pipeline for orthologue identification and matrix construction. The methods are standard in phylogenomics, with appropriate filtering steps and clear reporting of matrix characteristics. The tree-likeness scoring approach (C23) is properly cited to Misof et al., 2013.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis of the 430-gene matrix places Cnidaria and Placozoa as sister groups with full posterior probability under CAT+GTR+Γ4 (Bayesian) and with marginal support under C60+LG+FO+R4 (ML). This topology is robust to removal of newly-added placozoan genomes and shows little internal branch diversity within Placozoa.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 present the primary phylogenetic result with appropriate statistical support values and sensitivity analyses. The use of site-heterogeneous models (CAT+GTR) is appropriate for deep phylogenetic questions. The robustness test (C28) strengthens confidence that the result is not driven solely by the new data.

results.result: Quartet-based concordance analyses show no strong phylogenetic conflicts among gene trees, but internode certainty metrics near 0 for key clades including Cnidaria+Placozoa suggest that support for ancient relationships may be masked by gene-tree estimation errors.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 appropriately apply concordance metrics to assess gene tree conflict. The low internode certainty values (C30) indicate genuine uncertainty in the phylogenetic signal, which the authors correctly interpret as potentially reflecting gene-tree estimation error rather than true biological conflict. This nuanced interpretation is appropriate.

results.result: Compositional heterogeneity of amino-acid frequencies is a known source of phylogenetic error not modeled by CAT+GTR. Previous work shows placozoans and choanoflagellates deviate strongly from mean metazoan amino-acid composition, possibly due to GC content differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 correctly cite established knowledge about compositional bias as a systematic error source. The citations to multiple studies (C31) support this general principle, and the specific observation about placozoans/choanoflagellates (C32) is properly attributed to Nosenko et al., 2013. The speculation about GC content (C33) is appropriately tentative.

results.result: Dayhoff-6 recoding of the 430-gene matrix recovers full support for Cnidaria+Placozoa under CAT+GTR, with the only major topological change being Porifera (rather than Ctenophora) as sister to all other animals. Similar recoding effects have been observed in other studies and interpreted as evidence for compositional bias affecting Ctenophora placement.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 describe the effect of alphabet recoding on phylogenetic inference. The Dayhoff-6 recoding is a standard approach to mitigate compositional bias. The consistency with other studies (C36-C37) provides external validation. However, the interpretation that recoding necessarily corrects bias (rather than introducing different biases) remains debated in the field.

results.result: Multiple research groups have consistently reported strong support for Planulozoa (Cnidaria+Bilateria) under CAT+GTR. A 303-gene BUSCO matrix constructed in this study also shows full support for Planulozoa in both amino-acid and Dayhoff-6 recoded analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 accurately summarize prior literature and present new analyses that replicate the Planulozoa result. The BUSCO-based matrix (C39) provides an independent test using a different gene selection strategy, and the consistency with published work (C38) is well-documented with appropriate citations.

results.result: Both the 430-gene and 303-gene BUSCO matrices fail posterior predictive tests for compositional homogeneity, with the BUSCO matrix failing more severely (z-scores 330-340 vs 176-187). The difference in z-scores is largely attributable to placozoans, with additional contributions from choanoflagellates.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 present posterior predictive test results with specific quantitative values from Table 2 and Figure 3C. The tests appropriately assess model adequacy, and the identification of specific taxa driving compositional heterogeneity (C42) provides mechanistic insight. The more severe failure of the BUSCO matrix is notable and well-documented.

results.result: A null-simulation test identifies 55% (764/1388) of genes as compositionally biased at α=0.10. This test is less prone to Type II errors than the conventional χ² test.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 describe a rigorous test for compositional bias applied to individual genes. The high proportion of biased genes (55%) is striking and well-quantified. The citation to Foster, 2004 (C44) appropriately supports the methodological choice. The conservative α threshold strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: Genes passing the compositional bias test show strong support for Cnidaria+Placozoa, while genes failing the test show strong support for Cnidaria+Bilateria (Planulozoa).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 present the key experimental result demonstrating that phylogenetic signal depends on compositional bias. This is a direct test of the hypothesis that compositional heterogeneity drives support for Planulozoa. The opposing results from test-passing vs test-failing genes provide compelling evidence for systematic error. Figure 4 supports these claims.

results.result: In the test-failing matrix, CAT+GTR analysis supports Porifera-sister in both amino-acid and Dayhoff-6 alphabets, while profile mixture models support Ctenophora-sister. The difference between models need not reflect compositional heterogeneity, as both assume a single composition vector, but CAT+GTR better accommodates site-heterogeneous substitution patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 provide important insight into model differences. The observation that CAT+GTR and profile mixture models give different results even when both assume compositional homogeneity (C49) is well-reasoned and properly cited. This distinguishes compositional bias from other forms of model inadequacy.

results.result: Dayhoff-6 recoding impacts only the test-passing matrix, where it shifts support from Ctenophora-sister to Porifera-sister and diminishes support for Placozoa+Cnidaria, possibly reflecting information loss from alphabet reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 describe differential effects of recoding on the two gene sets. The observation that recoding affects test-passing but not test-failing genes is interesting and well-documented in Figure 4. The speculation about information loss (C51) is appropriately tentative and acknowledges the shorter matrix length as a potential confounding factor.

results.result: Mean trimmed alignment length may be a hidden variable related to phylogenetic discordance, with test-passing and 430-gene matrices having shorter alignments than test-failing and BUSCO matrices. Alignment length has been shown to predict other phylogenetically relevant metrics.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 identify a potential confounding variable but acknowledge uncertainty about its significance. While the correlation between alignment length and compositional bias test results is noted, no analysis is presented to determine whether length independently affects phylogenetic inference or is merely correlated with compositional properties. This requires further investigation.

results.result: The phylogenetic link between cnidarians and placozoans seen in compositionally unbiased gene sets requires further testing with other analyses and data modalities such as rare genomic changes.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 appropriately acknowledges that the Cnidaria+Placozoa result, while supported by the compositionally unbiased gene set, requires independent validation. This is a reasonable and scientifically conservative statement. The suggestion of rare genomic changes as an alternative data type is appropriate for testing deep phylogenetic relationships.

results.result: Support for Cnidaria+Bilateria can be assigned to compositional heterogeneity as a systematic error source. Depending on orthologue selection, strong support can be obtained for either Cnidaria+Placozoa or Cnidaria+Bilateria using site-heterogeneous models.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 summarize the main findings of the study. The demonstration that gene selection based on compositional bias testing yields opposing phylogenetic results (C71) provides strong evidence that compositional heterogeneity is a systematic error source (C70). This is the central contribution of the paper and is well-supported by the analyses in C43-C46.

results.result: The authors argue that placozoans should not be dismissed as irrelevant to understanding early bilaterian evolution despite their simplicity. They advocate for testing homology hypotheses by including placozoans in comparisons with cnidarians and bilaterians, noting recent methodological progress in placozoan research.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 present the authors' perspective on the evolutionary significance of placozoans. This is appropriately framed as interpretation rather than established fact. The citations to recent methodological advances (C59) support the feasibility of the proposed research agenda. The argument for equal consideration of placozoans as an outgroup (C57) is logically sound given the phylogenetic results.

results.result: If Cnidaria+Placozoa is correct, homologous characters between Bilateria and Cnidaria must have originated earlier in animal evolution and should either occur cryptically in placozoans or have been lost. This has implications for paleobiological scenarios and molecular clock estimates of early animal evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 present logical inferences from the phylogenetic hypothesis. The reasoning is sound: if placozoans are sister to Cnidaria+Bilateria, then shared cnidarian-bilaterian characters must predate the placozoan divergence (C60-C61). The implications for paleobiology (C62) are appropriately cited and represent reasonable consequences of the phylogenetic revision.

results.result: Placozoans are simple microscopic animals with six morphological cell types (though more are apparent via single-cell RNA-seq), lacking conventional organ systems but showing coordinated behavior. They reproduce asexually in lab conditions, with sexual reproduction remaining elusive despite genetic evidence of recombination.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 provide background on placozoan biology, all properly cited to primary literature. These are established facts about placozoan anatomy, physiology, and reproduction that contextualize the phylogenetic study. The citations are appropriate and the claims accurately represent current knowledge.

results.result: Early molecular analyses struggled to place Placozoa phylogenetically but revealed high cryptic diversity (up to 27% 16S rRNA divergence). A 2008 genome analysis supported Placozoa as sister to Cnidaria+Bilateria (Planulozoa) and revealed a surprisingly bilaterian-like developmental gene toolkit.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C13 accurately summarize prior work on placozoan phylogenetics and genomics, with appropriate citations. The paradox of simple morphology with complex gene content (C13) is well-established in the literature and properly attributed to Dunn et al., 2015. This provides essential context for the current study.

results.result: The major controversy in metazoan phylogenetics concerns whether Porifera or Ctenophora is sister to other animals. Different studies support different positions, with debates over artifacts, gene selection effects, and implications for trait evolution. New placozoan data have been slow to emerge during this controversy.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 provide comprehensive background on the Porifera vs Ctenophora debate with extensive appropriate citations. This contextualizes why resolving placozoan position matters and why compositional bias is a concern. The observation that placozoan data have lagged (C19) motivates the current study.
